records.bodyText:
Reply from East Lothian Council re Brownfield Site.......
In response to your email sent on the 28th of September, I would like to clarify that the requirements you mentioned i.e. for local authorities to prepare, maintain and publish registers of previously developed (brownfield) land is set out in The Town and Country Planning (Brownfield Land Register) Regulations 2017. This Regulation and also other policy requirements pertinent to the previously developed land included in NPPF apply to England and not to Scotland where a different planning regime is in place (the responsibility for planning matters was transferred to the Scottish parliament and Scottish Government under the Scotland Act 1998).
Regarding the site in question, I can confirm that this land is allocated in the East Lothian Local Development Plan (2018) under Proposal EGT1: Land at Former Cockenzie Power Station. This LDP Proposal states that “Land at Cockenzie may also present significant opportunities for renewable energy-related investment.”
The ELC Planning Service provides annual updates to The Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey (SVDLS) which is available at https://www.gov.scot/.../the-scottish-vacant-and.../ This survey is undertaken every year to establish the extent and state of vacant and derelict land in Scotland. According to our last year’s survey (2025) the site at the former coal yard at Cockenzie was classified as derelict as it is on previously developed land which has a physical constraint caused by its previous use which hampers its redevelopment.
As mentioned earlier the site is allocated in the current LDP and over the last years public funding has been secured towards the works aiming to remove the site’s physical constraints and changing its derelict classification.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
At last after 10 months, the Scottish Government has published the Onshore electricity generation - Electricity Act threshold: summary consultation responses.  This Consultation was in response to our Petition to the Scottish Parliament  which, among other things, requested that the current 50MW threshold be raised in order to allow more local decision making with Ministers focusing on the really major applications.  We also insisted that local rejection of a development must be a key material consideration in the decision making process.
We haven't scrutinised all of the responses yet but Q2 shows that the vast majority of respondents opted for raising the threshold to 150MW.  Development, Property and Land Management Sector and Agents were the only category who disagreed.  That was to be expected!
Great to see that so many of our members responded to the consultation.  
You can read the summary of responses here
GOV.SCOT Onshore electricity generation - Electricity Act threshold: summary consultation responses

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Thanks to Ria Parkinson for this summary of an article in the Times today.
A great article from Juliet Samuel in The Times highlighting the growing challenges NESO is facing keeping the lights on. After years of under-investment and wishful thinking around the energy transition, we’re relying more and more on renewables, interconnectors and batteries which can abruptly "turn off and on" with little, to no notice. The old system of large, steady fossil plants was far easier to balance. Juliet writes that engineers are starting to sound the alarm that margins are getting tight, and that a number of recent frequency excursions and interconnector limit breaches aren’t helping the “nothing to see here” message either.
THETIMES.COM Why are power grid bosses gaslighting us?

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
Juliet Samuel had an excellent and comprehensive piece in the Times yesterday on the recent grid shenanigans; it's entitled 'Why are power grid bosses gaslighting us?'
She said:  As for today, whenever you’re reading this, who knows what fun lies in store for the control room?
Well, Juliet - we're a day late, but we can tell you what's happening this morning, thanks to David Turver who tweeted that frequency was going up and down like a yoyo - our words, not his. 
What he said was:  And even more frequency oscillations this morning. Frequency above normal operating limit at 6:05, below from 7:14 to 7:22 and then above again from 7:32 to 7:34.  Curiouser and curiouser
Kathryn Porter has just tweeted this:
It's getting embarrassing now... This morning  @neso_energy
has blown through the intraday interconnector trading limits again and like yesterday the frequency has been above and below the safe operational limits
Margins are perfectly fine so I can only think this is a combination of poor modelling and forecasting and the grid constraints affecting the SE
Yesterday saw record balancing costs of just under £50 million so this isn't just a curiosity, it's chaos that's driving bills higher (balancing costs are part of network costs)
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columnists/article/why-are-power-grid-bosses-gaslighting-us-zk5q7ftfm?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Times%20Politics%20-%20Thursday%20October%2015&utm_term=audience_POLITICS
'The first thing to know is that this is not normal. The people who run Britain’s electricity grid want you to think it is, but it isn’t. I believe the psychological term is gaslighting, but given the impending winter gas shortage, that’s optimistic.
The facts are these. In the past fortnight there have been four, maybe five, highly unusual events in the control room of Britain’s electricity grid: major forecasting errors, formal calls to the market for extra power and demands for “emergency assistance” from our neighbours in Europe.
Senior managers at the publicly owned National Energy System Operator (Neso) want you to believe these incidents are “routine”. Since the last “routine” incident in June, which is now the subject of both a technical and a legal investigation, Neso has signed PR contracts worth £400,000 to convince everyone they are doing splendidly. What they haven’t done is learn any lessons or produce any in-depth analysis of what the hell is going on.
Yet things keep happening. On September 28, Neso’s forecasts showed it was going to run out of power and it had to put out a call for extra, same-day (and expensive) generation. After about 15 hours, it cancelled the notice — its forecasts were wrong. On October 6, it issued another call. Luckily, even though the wind was low, demand was lower. Again, the forecasts were wrong.
On October 9, for no obvious reason, the grid suddenly ran so short of power that its frequency, or “heartbeat”, went out of the normal operating range for ten minutes, which is what happened in June. An internal “frequency event report” on the latest incident, which I’ve seen thanks to a concerned insider, shows that Neso had to push more power from north to south than the wires are meant to take.
It also had to offer a fortune to incentivise power production from generators in the south. When even that wasn’t enough, it issued a call for “emergency assistance” from France. A Neso engineer says we were one circuit trip away from a very serious situation. “All that was left was [to] scramble for emergency assistance from the EU, violate transmission constraints or disconnect demand.”
Incredibly, three days later, Neso was begging France again, issuing its biggest-ever call for power.
Despite plentiful wind on October 12, with cable maintenance slightly overrunning, power couldn’t get down to meet demand in the south. The next day, Tuesday, the grid’s frequency first spiked too high and then fell too low, for reasons as yet unknown. As for today, whenever you’re reading this, who knows what fun lies in store for the control room?
Given how often Neso is being caught off guard, I suppose you could argue this is indeed now “routine”. As Andrew Larkins, an energy consultant and former Ofgem adviser, politely puts it: “They’re at risk of normalising something that’s meant to be part of an emergency system … It shows how hard they’re having to work to keep the lights on.” Winter hasn’t even started yet.
Why is this happening? The technical answer is we don’t know because Neso isn’t opening up the incidents to scrutiny in the way that, say, an airliner is forced to facilitate an industry-wide post-mortem when an engine chokes. More successful modernising grids, such as Australia’s, take the opposite approach.
The broader answer is that governments, regulators and owners of the system have indulged a decade of wishful thinking and under-investment, pretending they know how to pull off a radical energy transition when they have devoted appallingly little forethought, planning and money to the question.
The electricity grid used to run off a hundred or so fossil fuel generators, which can be turned up and down on request and are mechanically stable because they spin big, heavy rotors. Demand also tended to follow a pattern. This made balancing power supply and demand fairly straightforward.
Now, large portions of our power (some days, all of it) come from a mix of undersea cables, renewables plants and batteries, all of which can abruptly and unpredictably turn off and on. Small units, such as rooftop solar, don’t even send data to the grid. Customers are using new, variable gadgets like smart meters and electric cars. Forecasting and responding to changes has become, to be technical, a total bloody nightmare. “We can’t see how much reserve we have,” says the engineer.
On top of this, you have a regulator and grid operator moving at the pace of a Siberian town clerk in a Chekhov play. The grid code, which specifies the grid’s technical requirements, is so out of date that when Neso discovered hundreds of wind farms had their meters fitted backwards, so they tell the grid they’re consuming when they’re actually generating, there was no one obvious to blame. But a single technical change to the code can take years of consultations and meetings.
The rules governing grid stability are similarly out of date. A programme to install more granular sensors to monitor frequency in dozens of locations is well overdue. While the US grids have for years had 2,500 such sensors, Britain’s ambition is to have 40 (a tenth of what Larkins says would be equivalent coverage), and even some of those aren’t sharing data in a useable form. A working group on protocols to stop cascades of generator trips, which took out the solar-reliant Iberian grid last year, is crawling along.
It isn’t all Neso’s fault. Private owners of grid infrastructure are in no hurry to make unprofitable improvements. But nor are they being hurried or penalised. Ofgem has repeatedly tolerated grid regulatory failings and delayed or refused investment proposals. As a result, Neso, which ultimately passes costs to users, must now pay a fortune to buy in power on the day it’s needed to avoid blackouts.
Meanwhile, plans to manage the new power system assume we can use advanced software to fine-tune supply and demand. For example, the commercial fridge industry says it can tweak power use up or down. Brilliant! Except that hackers got at supermarket fridges in France this week and cranked them up to 50 degrees. It spoilt a lot of food. If we’re not careful, a hack like that could spoil the grid.
Governments, regulators, operators and owners have all conspired in the delusion that everything is fine and we can keep going at breakneck speed to “clean power 2030”. But the strain is showing and the engineers won’t pretend any more. You can’t run an electricity grid on a news grid.'
